title: The continuous Jacobian ideal of a geometrically regular affinoid quotient is the unit ideal
statement:
Let $K$ be a field complete for a nontrivial real-valued nonarchimedean absolute value and let $r,s\geq0$. Put $A=K\langle x_1,\ldots,x_r\rangle$, the ring of series $\sum_\nu a_\nu x^\nu$ with coefficients tending to zero (for every $\epsilon>0$, only finitely many have $|a_\nu|\geq\epsilon$). Choose $f_1,\ldots,f_s\in A$, put $I=(f_1,\ldots,f_s)$ and $C=A/I$, and write a bar for the image in $C$. Suppose that for every isometric embedding $K\hookrightarrow L$ into a complete real-valued nonarchimedean field, the ring $L\langle x_1,\ldots,x_r\rangle/(f_{1,L},\ldots,f_{s,L})$ is regular Noetherian [def-weil-regular-scheme], where $f_{j,L}$ is given by coefficient extension. For subsets $E\subseteq\{1,\ldots,s\}$ and $T\subseteq\{1,\ldots,r\}$ with $|E|=|T|$, order each by its natural order, set $I_E=(f_j:j\in E)$, and define
$$D_{E,T}=\det\bigl(\partial f_j/\partial x_i\bigr)_{i\in T,j\in E}\in A,\qquad (I_E:I)=\{a\in A:aI\subseteq I_E\}.$$
Here partial derivatives are termwise continuous derivatives of restricted series, and determinant is [def-weil-pbc-matrix-determinant]; the empty determinant is $1$ and $I_\varnothing=0$. Then the ideal
$$H=\sum_{E,T}\overline{(I_E:I)}\,\overline{D_{E,T}}\,C$$
is the unit ideal $C$. This includes the zero quotient and requires no fixed relative dimension.

proof.text: If $C=0$, every ideal of $C$ is the unit ideal. Otherwise fix any maximal ideal $\mathfrak m\subset C$ and let $\mathfrak n\subset A$ be its inverse image. The quotient map identifies $A/\mathfrak n=C/\mathfrak m=: \kappa$, a field, so $\mathfrak n$ is maximal and contains $I$. By [lem-per-affinoid-residual-conormal-injective], the continuous derivative map $d_{\mathfrak n}:I/\mathfrak n I\to\kappa^r$ is injective. Its hypotheses are precisely the field-extension hypotheses of the item; no perfectness or discretely valued assumption is added.

source.place: Proposition 3.3.2 proof, printed pp.20--21, the continuous conormal criterion and the choice of independent defining equations at a maximal ideal

proof.text: The classes of the $f_j$ span $I/\mathfrak n I$: writing $g=\sum_j a_jf_j$ and reducing the coefficients modulo $\mathfrak n$ proves this. Apply [lem-weil-span-independent-subfamily] to this finite spanning family and obtain $E\subseteq\{1,\ldots,s\}$ whose classes form a basis. Consequently the map $\kappa^E\to\kappa^r$ with columns $d_{\mathfrak n}([f_j])$, $j\in E$, is injective: a relation maps to zero only when its basis combination is zero.

source.place: Proposition 3.3.2 proof, printed pp.20--21, the continuous conormal criterion and the choice of independent defining equations at a maximal ideal

proof.text: Set $R=A_{\mathfrak n}$, whose maximal ideal is $\mathfrak nR$ by [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime], and let $M=(A\setminus\mathfrak n)^{-1}I$, with the fraction convention of [def-weil-pbc-module-localization]. This module is generated by the $f_j/1$. Its residue quotient is $I/\mathfrak n I$: the isomorphism sends the residue of $g/u$ to $(u\bmod\mathfrak n)^{-1}[g]$. The inverse sends $[g]$ to the residue of $g/1$; since $u\bmod\mathfrak n$ is a nonzero field element, both composites are the identity. Thus the basis from Step 2 spans $M/\mathfrak nRM$. By [lem-weil-pbc-nakayama-local-generators], the elements $f_j/1$, $j\in E$, generate $M$.

source.place: Proposition 3.3.2 proof, printed pp.20--21, the continuous conormal criterion and the choice of independent defining equations at a maximal ideal

proof.text:
For each $1\leq l\leq s$, Step 3 writes $f_l/1=\sum_{j\in E}(a_{lj}/u_{lj})(f_j/1)$ with $u_{lj}
otin\mathfrak n$. Multiplying by the finite product $v_l=\prod_{j\in E}u_{lj}$ gives an element $g_l=v_lf_l-\sum_{j\in E}b_{lj}f_j\in I$ whose localization is zero, where $b_{lj}\in A$. By the zero criterion in [def-weil-pbc-module-localization], some $w_l
otin\mathfrak n$ has $w_lg_l=0$ in $I$. Hence $h_l=w_lv_l
otin\mathfrak n$ and $h_lf_l\in I_E$. Put $a=\prod_{l=1}^s h_l$, using empty product $1$. Then $a
otin\mathfrak n$ and $af_l\in I_E$ for every $l$, whence $aI\subseteq I_E$. Thus $a\in(I_E:I)$. This proves the required colon membership directly, without invoking a flat-base-change theorem for colon ideals.

source.place: Proposition 3.3.2 proof, printed pp.20--21, the continuous conormal criterion and the choice of independent defining equations at a maximal ideal

proof.text: Apply [lem-weil-pbc-field-injective-matrix-nonzero-maximal-minor] to the injective matrix from Step 2, with $|E|$ columns and $r$ rows, ordering $E$ increasingly. It gives $|E|\leq r$ and a subset $T\subseteq\{1,\ldots,r\}$ of size $|E|$ with determinant nonzero in $\kappa$. This determinant is $D_{E,T}\bmod\mathfrak n$: the finite Leibniz sum defining the determinant in [def-weil-pbc-matrix-determinant] commutes with reduction of every entry. Thus $D_{E,T}\notin\mathfrak n$. The same argument includes $E=T=\varnothing$, where the determinant is $1$.

source.place: Proposition 3.3.2 proof, printed pp.20--21, the continuous conormal criterion and the choice of independent defining equations at a maximal ideal

proof.text: The element $\bar a\,\overline{D_{E,T}}$ belongs to $H$ by its defining sum. Its residue in $C/\mathfrak m=A/\mathfrak n$ is the product of two nonzero field elements by Steps 4--5, so it is outside $\mathfrak m$. We have proved that $H$ is contained in no maximal ideal of $C$. If $H\neq C$, [lem-weil-pbc-proper-ideal-contained-in-maximal] would give a maximal ideal containing $H$, a contradiction. Hence $H=C$. The selected cardinality $|E|$ may vary with $\mathfrak m$, so no equidimensionality is used.
